chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruttani (திருத்தணிகை, 3 of 5): the poet counts his numberless births and deaths, takes apart the body as a pot, bellows and bag of humours, turns from courtesans, flattering court poetry and barren book-learning, and asks for the feet as the raft over the seas of desire, birth and learning; the praise names Murugan as the southern guru who told Siva the meaning of Om, and Thiruttani as Sivaloka, where he is physician of the disease of birth.
structure_note: Births and deeds counted (270); the body and the humours (274, 275, 280); courtesans and desire (273, 276, 281, 282, 283); self-abuse and the plea not to be cast off (272); against court poets who flatter patrons (271) and against learning that scorns the wise (279); samsara and the gift of praise (277); short prayers for grace (278, 284).

270.reading: The poet asks how many bodies, countless as grains of sand, he has filled, how many lives born in the sea like shoals of fish, on hills and in springs, how many times infatuation for women held him and Death snatched his life, how many deceits he thought, families he ruined and lives he killed like a beast; and he asks Murugan to grace this fool, rough and wretched, to melt at the flower feet. The praise, in a long run of drum syllables, shows the vel in the battlefield where kites and jackals feed, and Thiruttani where Siva's devotees and sages worship with honeyed flowers.
270.nuance: The plea is a catalogue built on எத்தனை, 'how many', closing with அளவேதோ and அளவிலை, 'what measure? there is none': the poet counts his births and his sins alike. The first words (சினத்திலத்தினை) are hard to divide, and விதிகர may be the deeds fate ordains.

271.reading: The poet asks to leave the delusion of the poets who praise base patrons as equal to the rain cloud, the treasure of Kubera, the wish-cow and the wish-tree, melting their own minds before them, and who steal and twist old verses of rare meaning to make poems, so that he may sing instead of Murugan's kuvalai hill. The praise shows Murugan himself, wounded by the poison-tipped blue arrows of Valli's eyes under her dark bow-brows, falling at the feet of the doe's daughter crying 'refuge' and melting in infatuation to embrace her.
271.nuance: A satire of court poetry: the patron is likened to cloud, padma-nidhi, Kamadhenu and kalpaka tree, the stock comparisons for a giver, and the poems are plagiarised (பழைய மொழியைத் திருடி நெருடி). The praise reverses the plea: the god falls at a girl's feet crying அபயம், as the poet will not fall at a patron's. உழையின் மகள் is Valli as a doe's daughter.

272.reading: The poet heaps names on himself: a rat-snake for quarrels, one who eats without witness, far from the shastra of holy ash, a sinner without the meaning of austerity, a dog barking Tamil who does not think of Murugan with love as poets do, a traitor who does not honour the wise, a wretch flowering with the three malas; he asks whether it is Murugan's duty to cast him off, and whether there is no state to be gained by going with the devotees. The praise tells at length of Surpanakha's nose cut off and Ravana carrying Sita away, and names Murugan nephew of Rama the archer who destroyed him, at Thiruttani with its long spring of kazhuneer.
272.nuance: போக்கிவிடக் கடனோ: 'is it your duty to throw me away?', a challenge as much as a plea. அடியாரொடு போய்ப் பெறுகைக்கு இலையோ கதி: the hope is to be saved in the company of devotees, not alone. Several of the epithets (சாரை, சாக்ஷியறப் பசியாறி, வ்ருதாவன்) are obscure, and the source seems damaged in தவ்முழ்குந்.

273.reading: The poet asks whether he will wander caught in the winking ways of lust, bewildered by thieving, hollow, proud women who dance daily, sway their bodies and cast the net of their eyes, letting what is good run out of his mind. The praise names Murugan the able child who told the meaning of the great Om (மாகுடிலை) to the ash-smeared, babbling madman Siva, the supreme who comes in compassion to the wise, the southern guru skilled in a thousand yogas, the slayer of Sura in a field of ghouls, and the lord of Thiruttani, whose spring holds a lily that blooms three times a day.
273.nuance: குடிலை is a name for the pranava, so the Om teaching is explicit here. தெக்ஷிண குருநாதா, the southern guru, gives Murugan the title of Dakshinamurti, Siva's own teaching form. Siva is called பித்தன், the madman, a devotional epithet.

274.reading: The poet asks not to be born again in the world through desire for this sinful body, steeped in the delusion of the three gunas, wrapped in skin and soaked in Kama's sickness, and to be given the grace that neither cheats nor the proud can reach. The praise names Murugan who removes the deeds of those who sing and serve without fail, who destroyed Sura, the true wisdom of Thanigai, the one who embraces the girl of candied-milk speech, and calls him father, eternal, free and knowing.
274.nuance: The song is in clipped syllables (துப்பா ரப்பா டற்றீ), so the first lines are hard to divide and the reading of the body's description is tentative. அத்தா நித்தா முத்தா சித்தா: four titles in a rhyme, father, eternal, freed, knower. எத்தார் வித்தாரத்தே கிட்டா அருள்: grace is beyond both deceivers and the learned show-offs.

275.reading: The poet asks whether a day will come when this body falls: a hut of skin, the pot of pleasure and pain, of mala and maya, of the humours, of babbling speech, unable to grasp the many sect books, bound with flesh and blood, loathsome, in which he wanders seeking. The praise names Murugan worshipped by gurus who wear rudraksha and ash, lord of the twelve hills and Thanigai, son of Parvati and the river, who helps the ascetics, easy to reach for those who praise him in Tamil verse and hard for those who do not.
275.nuance: சட்டவாக்கு அழிவது ஒருநாளே: the plea is for the body's end, not its health. The praise closes on a paired rule, எத்திடார்க்கு அரிய, முத்த பாத் தமிழ் கொடு எத்தினார்க்கு எளிய: the Lord is hard for those who do not praise and easy for those who praise in Tamil. The crowded first lines (காற் பதலை, கைக்கொளாக் கதறு) are hard to divide.

276.reading: The poet heaps names on the women who sell their breasts for a price, shaking, scheming, blind, deceitful, slippery, and asks not to enter their net, nor to play with those who call men coral-red and bangled; he asks whether a day will come when the states of consciousness and the tattvas perish, the darkness is cleared, a single light spreads, grace is fed to him and the paired feet given. The praise names Uma the emerald-formed, who creates all and with the dancer removes it, as Murugan's mother, Vishnu with discus and conch who swallowed the earth as his uncle, and the peacock that circles the world in a moment, at Thiruttani with Valli and Devayanai.
276.nuance: விலைமுலை: breasts sold for a price, which makes these courtesans in the trade sense. The plea is in the language of Saiva doctrine: அவத்தை தத்துவம் அழிபட, இருள் அறை விலக்கு, ஒரு சுடரொளி பரவ. The praise gives Uma the dance at the summit of the Supreme (பரத்தின் உச்சியில் நடம் நவிலும் உமை).

277.reading: The poet asks for grace so that, instead of plunging into the unstable sea of samsara and calling it real, labouring long, hiding from the great, failing to praise the feet, steeped in bodily disease and the sickness of birth and maddened, he may seek out and cut the root of birth, chant Murugan's name and be saved; he asks Murugan to keep him, a servant who seeks him as companion, in joy, since that is his duty, and to let those who worship him live praising him with the Thiruppugazh. The praise names Murugan Valli's bridegroom, and the lord of Thiruttani, which is like Sivaloka, the physician of the disease of birth.
277.nuance: பவரோக வயித்திய நாத: Murugan as Vaidyanatha, physician of the disease of becoming, which matches the plea's பவநோய். கடனாகும் இது: as in 272, the poet tells the Lord that saving him is his duty. The song names its own book (திருப்புகழ் கூறி).

278.reading: A short prayer: the poet asks that whatever he thinks not fail, that he not be parted from the steadied mind, that he not perish in the great tattvas, and that he be given the eternal consciousness that rises. The praise names Murugan easy for men and devotees, great in the three Tamils, the youngest of the sons born to Siva, at Thiruttani.
278.nuance: நித்திய சித்து: eternal consciousness, the soul's goal named in a single phrase. மிலைத்த புத்தி may mean the mind that has been crowned or fixed; the sense of the first two lines is uncertain.

279.reading: The poet, who feeds his body day and night through the senses, has read some old Vedas, new books and many Puranas, and calls those settled in the reality whose breadth and length cannot be measured 'fools and dumb', asks whether he must perish without knowledge. The praise shows the vel thrown so that the mountain broke, Brahma was humbled, Indra freed from prison, the dark sea cried out and the great mango tree scattered, and names the chest adorned with kazhuneer, jasmine and kadamba at Thanigai.
279.nuance: The confession is of learning that breeds contempt: reading some Vedas and Puranas, the poet mocked the silent knowers as அசடர் மூகர், fools and mutes, when their silence was the knowledge. அகல நீளம் என்று அளவு கூறரும் பொருள்: the Reality whose breadth and length cannot be told.

280.reading: The poet takes apart his body: a head of big teeth, hands and feet that bear it, a false pot, a place of blame, a belly-pot for hunger, an artificial bellows full of bile, bound by the three humours and the five senses, a bag of disease; he asks Murugan to give him the purpose that would cut off its birth. The praise names the hero who sets on his true feet those devotees who speak from the heart, the embracer of the hunter girl, the golden son of Siva who burnt the three cities with a laugh, at Thiruttani, renowned for the Tamil of dharma.
280.nuance: பசிக்குடற் கடம், கிருத்திமத் துருத்தி, இப்பிணிப்பை: pot, bellows and bag, the same images as 258. முக்குற்றம் is probably the three humours of medicine (wind, bile, phlegm), which would make பித்து bile rather than madness. The plea asks not for health but for the end of the birth that makes such a body.

281.reading: The poet describes women who recall old intimacy, call sweetly, embrace, leave nail-marks, press face to face, feed a man with their spittle and work base magic, women who say they are many men's; he asks whether a day will come when Murugan sets him, a fool who longed for their ruinous work, disgraced and lost, at his red-gold feet, which make all powers and the eight siddhis easy and plain. The praise shows ghouls dancing in the battlefield and Sura vomiting blood, and Murugan stroking the feet of Valli in her leaf skirt, touching the tilaka on her round face and fastening a golden bodice over her breasts on the Thani hill.
281.nuance: குத்திர வித்தை: base arts, probably love-charms or drugs, the deceit of the women. The praise inverts the plea: the poet asks to be set at the Lord's feet, and the Lord himself strokes Valli's feet (பதத்துணை வருடி). The feet that make the siddhis easy suggest the siddhis are a by-product, not the goal.

282.reading: The poet calls himself the foolish wretch who rolls embracing women with knitted brows, sweating and thrilled, caught in their eyes, the evil base man who has lost the guru's word and abandoned the way of release, and asks whether Murugan will not think to let him praise the victorious lotus feet. The praise names the vel that ended the false race of demons, the chest joined to Valli, and the beautiful lord (சொக்கப் பெருமாள்) on the pure Thani hill where drums sound daily.
282.nuance: குருமொழி அற்று: what the poet has lost is the teacher's word, so desire is cast as a failure of instruction. The question turns to the Lord: கருதாதோ, will you not think of it, rather than asking what the poet should do.

283.reading: The poet speaks of women whose eyes, like a sharpened sword, rush to the ears, cut and pierce and steal pleasure, and asks that he not perish exhausted in desire, confusion and sorrow over them, but be granted to praise the fresh-flowered golden feet of the Vedas and be happy. The praise names Murugan who comes on the gem-necked peacock so that the devotees of his fragrant feet do not perish in the prison of women's eyes, the husband of the golden hunter girl, and the lord at the blue hill.
283.nuance: The whole song is about the eyes: in the plea they are a sword that cuts to the ears, in the praise a prison (மாதர் கண் சிறை) from which the Lord comes to free his devotees. சொற்கருத்தர் at the close may mean the lord of those who hold his word in mind.

284.reading: The poet asks not to whirl in the sea of desire for the breasts of scheming women, in the unending sea of the womb, or in the sea of the many arts, but to be given the raft of Murugan's kadamba-garlanded, anklet-bright feet. The praise shows Brahma imprisoned, the fourteen worlds living, the seven seas and seven mountains shaken, and the vel taken up in war on the proud peacock, at Thiruttani of wisdom and the three Tamils.
284.nuance: Three seas, of desire (ப்ரியக்கடல்), birth (கருக்கடல்) and learning (கலைக்கடல்), and one raft, the feet (கழற்புணை). Learning is placed beside desire and birth as something to drown in.

links.note: The Kural makes the Lord's feet the way across the great sea of births; 284 makes them a raft (புணை) and adds two more seas to cross, desire for women and the arts of learning.
Both say learning without knowledge of the Lord leaves one a fool; 279 confesses it in the first person, having read Vedas and Puranas and mocked the silent knowers as dumb.
Both measure the Lord by breadth and length and find no measure: Tirumular asks who knows them, and 279 names the reality whose breadth and length cannot be told, which the poet's learning scorned.
Both take the body apart as a false pot, a bellows and a home of diseases, and both ask not for health but for the end of the birth that brings such a body.
Both make the Thiruppugazh itself what saves: 269 gives it the power to end birth, and 277 asks that devotees live speaking it without forgetting.

The Tirumanthiram says the soul is born and dies again through much folly (பிறந்தும் இறந்தும் பல் பேதைமையாலே) until, renouncing, Siva's grace becomes its light. 270 counts the same round, how many bodies, how many times Death took his life (எத்தனை ... நமன் உயிர் பறிகொள்வது அளவேதோ), and names himself the fool whose mind is ruined (மசகனை ... மதியழி விரகனை). Both put the cause of the endless births in folly, and look to grace to end it.

271 renounces the poets who liken base patrons to the pouring cloud, Kubera's padma treasure, the wish-cow and the wish-tree (சொரியு முகிலைப் பதும நிதியைச் சுரபி தருவை). 292 confesses having done this himself, comparing poor men to the cloud, the sun and the divine tree (முகிலும் இரவியும் ... தெய்வதரு நிகரென). The two songs quote the same list of a patron-poem, once as satire of others and once as the poet's own begging (இரவு).

The Kural makes the rain cloud (மாரி) the figure of a giver who seeks no return: what does the world give back to it? 271 mocks poets who call a base patron the pouring cloud (சொரியு முகில்). The Kural's image of true giving is the stock flattery the song refuses to sing.

The Tirumanthiram tells of going with the devotees of the Lord's devotees (அடியார் அடியாருடன் போய்) into his city, where the gatekeepers announce him and the Lord says 'let him come'. 272, after heaping abuse on himself, asks whether there is no state to be gained by going with the devotees (அடியாரொடு போய்ப் பெறுகைக்கு இலையோ கதி). The song's hope is the arrival the Tirumanthiram describes: the unworthy man is admitted in the company of devotees.

274 asks for the grace that எத்தார் and the showy (வித்தாரத்தே) cannot reach (கிட்டா எட்டா அருள்); 275 closes on the Lord hard for those who do not praise and easy for those who praise in Tamil (எத்திடார்க்கு அரிய ... எத்தினார்க்கு எளிய). If எத்தார் is read as ஏத்தார், those who do not praise, rather than cheats, the two neighbouring songs make the same rule about who can reach the Lord.

275 and 298 end on the same line: the Lord hard for those who do not praise and easy for those who praise him with pure Tamil verse (எத்திடார்க்கு அரிய முத்தபாத் தமிழ்கொடு எத்தினார்க்கு எளிய பெருமாளே). The repeat is a near-identical refrain; 275 sets it after a plea for the loathsome body to fall, 298 after a plea to let go of the household before Death.

The Tirumanthiram says that by grace the five states cease to work and the five malas leave like evening darkness before a flame (சுடர்முனம் அந்தி இருள்போலும் ஐம்மலம் மாறுமே). 276 asks for the day when the states and tattvas perish (அவத்தை தத்துவம் அழிபட), the darkness is driven off and a single light spreads (இருளறை விலக்கு வித்தொரு சுடரொளி பரவ). The song's plea uses the Tirumanthiram's doctrine and its image of darkness ended by a flame.

276 asks that the tattvas perish (தத்துவம் அழிபட); 278 asks that he not perish in the great tattvas (கனத்த தத்துவம் உற்று அழியாமல்). The two neighbouring songs use the same verb with the tattvas in opposite directions: the bonds are to be destroyed so that the soul is not destroyed by them.

The Tirumanthiram calls the Lord companion on the way and medicine (வழித்துணையாய் மருந்தாய் இருந்தார்). 277 names the poet a servant who seeks Murugan as companion (உனைத் துணைதேடும் அடியேனை) and calls Murugan physician of the disease of birth (பவரோக வயித்திய நாத), against the sickness of becoming (பவநோய்) in the plea. Both join the two roles, companion and cure, in the one Lord.

The Tirumanthiram calls the body a bag (காயப்பை) of the senses and the bound inner faculties, which the Lord ties and unties. 280 calls it this bag of disease bound by the three humours and the senses (முக்குற்றத் தொடைப் புலனாலும் பிணித்த இப்பிணிப்பை) and asks for the purpose that cuts off its birth. The same bag, tied by the senses, is described by one as the Lord's work and by the other as something to be ended.

The Tirumanthiram says that seeking the Lord's feet without fault, the eight great siddhis are not hard for him (அரியது எனக்கில்லை அட்டமா சித்தி) because the Lord cut off his birth. 281 asks to be set at the red-gold feet by which all powers and the eight siddhis become easy (அகில சத்தியும் எட்டுறு சித்தியும் எளிதென). Both make the siddhis follow from the feet rather than be sought for themselves.

The Tirumanthiram says clarity is seeing the guru's form, saying his name, hearing his holy words (குருவின் திருவார்த்தை கேட்டல்) and thinking on him. 282 calls himself the evil man who has lost the guru's word and so abandoned the way of release (குருமொழி அற்றுக் கதிதனை விட்டிட்டிடு தீயக் கயவன்). The song shows the Tirumanthiram's rule from the other side: without the guru's word, desire takes the place of clarity.

The Kural's lover says the girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும்). 283 makes women's eyes a sharpened sword that rushes to the ears, cuts and pierces (வடிகூர் வாள் போல ... வெட்டித் தொளைத்து), and the Lord a rescuer from the prison of women's eyes (மாதர்கள் கண் சிறை). The killing eye the Kural admires the song asks to be saved from.

The Kural's lovesick woman says the sea of desire certainly exists and the safe raft to cross it does not (ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்). 284 names the seas of desire, birth and learning (ப்ரியக்கடல், கருக்கடல், கலைக்கடல்) and asks for a raft, the anklet-bright feet (கழற்புணை). The song answers the Kural's despair with a raft, on condition it is the Lord's.

The Naladiyar says learning has no shore (கல்வி கரையில) while the learner's days are few, so one must choose what is fitting, like the bird that leaves the water and drinks the milk. 284 puts the sea of the many arts (அநேகங் கலைக்கடல்) beside the seas of desire and birth as one more sea to whirl in. The Naladiyar's shoreless learning becomes in the song something to be crossed, not sifted.

source_issues: Song 272: தவ்முழ்குந் (line 3) and மற்றவ்ரு தாவனை (line 7) look damaged, perhaps for தவம் மூழ்கும் and வ்ருதாவன், though not flagged.
Song 276: அனைததையும் (line 13) is a typo for அனைத்தையும்.
Song 277: one corrupt character, in அதனு஡டே (line 2), read as அதனூடே.
Song 278: மதித் முத்தமிழிற் (line 6) has lost a letter, probably மதித்த.
Song 284: three corrupt characters, in கடலு஡டும் (lines 4, 5 and 6), each read as கடலூடும்.
